extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, scholarly publishing staff, and authors/researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how journals should design author-facing guidelines and manuscript submission systems to reduce burden on authors and harmonize processes across publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal guidelines should be simple and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Several authors discussed having to deal with conflicting, hidden, incomplete, or unclear guidelines, and some said that journals should share templates so that it is easier for authors to adhere to journal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes and evidence: “Submission guidelines of journals are sometimes ambiguous and I am lost how to interpret them.” 66% of respondents said they found guidelines unclear, incomplete, or both. A study of 80 journals showed many do not clearly provide needed information; journals scored better on formatting clarity than on submission/post-submission processes and ethical requirements. Recommend regular review and improvement of guidelines from authors' perspective, especially non–English-speaking authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting requirements should be standardized/harmonized
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common view was the need to have standard guidelines across journals because of the difficulty in adapting manuscripts to different formatting requirements when they are prepared for submission to a new journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-suggested approaches: stick to a handful of accepted styles (MLA, APA, Vancouver, etc.), or an international style; integrate differing rules for references/terminology. Notes that some publishers have adopted format-flexible policies (Elsevier's Your Paper Your Way; Taylor & Francis' Format-Free Submission), but industry-wide standardization is lacking. Recognize reasons for diversity (discipline, journal size/resources, readership, stylistic preference) but advocate for harmonization at least within broad disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission systems need to be universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Many authors reported the need to create and manage multiple accounts for multiple journal submissions and suggested a universal system (or similar systems) to submit manuscripts and track their status across journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific suggestions: integrated systems allowing single account across journals, automatic entry of author metadata (name, affiliation, contact), similar processes across systems to be author-friendly. Acknowledge complexity of implementing universal systems and that lack of standardization hampers practical solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too much time is wasted in journal submission and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors feel time spent on formatting is unproductive and adds little value; some argue journals should not demand total compliance with formatting at submission when fate of manuscript is uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and framing: authors call formatting requirements 'absurdly complicated' and a 'huge time sink'. Conservative estimate cited: 4 hours to format/submit a single manuscript, implying ~1,370 years of global researcher time annually. Recommendation: scrutinize submission/formatting requirements, prioritize what is critical at submission, and shift nonessential burdens away from authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a checklist that fully discloses and organizes all formatting requirements in a logical order
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide a checklist that fully discloses and organizes all formatting requirements in a logical order. Journals should not hide additional formatting requirements inside the submission window or sections thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: disclose all requirements in one place so authors aren't surprised by hidden instructions during submission; avoid scattering instructions between website and submission interface; a clear checklist reduces ambiguity and perceived unprofessionalism when authors miss buried rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow format-free submission / indicate format does not affect editorial decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals have clarified that format does not affect their editorial decision as long as a manuscript has all the required components; some publishers have adopted policies that do not require authors to follow any specific manuscript format at the time of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Elsevier's Your Paper Your Way; Taylor & Francis' Format-Free Submission. Guidance is to consider permitting flexible initial formats and only enforcing strict formatting after acceptance to reduce wasted author effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Which guidelines are absolutely important for authors to follow at the time of submission? Those that are not can be omitted and taken care of after manuscripts are accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should identify and document the minimum essential criteria (e.g., manuscript components, completeness of information, critical submission-system fields) that must be satisfied before processing; discourage requiring more than these at submission. Criteria may vary by broad discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the guidelines worded carefully so as to be understood easily by researchers for whom the journal will be of interest, especially non–English-speaking researchers? Are any guidelines potentially ambiguous or conflicting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate wording for ambiguity, consistency across pages and submission interface, and accessibility for non-native English speakers. Regularly revise wording and test with target author groups to reduce interpretation gaps noted between authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Have all the guidelines been provided in a logical fashion in one place? Are any manuscript-specific instructions missing on the website but provided only when the author uses the submission system?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist: consolidate all instructions on an author guidelines page; avoid hiding instructions inside the submission workflow; ensure formatting, submission, post-submission, and ethics instructions are all present and logically organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of existing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of enforcing unique styles and preferences (e.g., for references, nomenclature/terminology), can the journal simply adopt common and already existing standards that best suit its needs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adopting widely used reference styles, nomenclature standards, and community norms rather than inventing unique variants. This reduces friction for authors and aids interoperability with tools and conversion pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time
rubrics_metrics.description: How much time would it take a first-time author to prepare a manuscript per the journal guidelines or navigate the submission system? For authors’ benefit, journals might consider providing an estimate of this time on their author guidelines page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend journals estimate and publish typical preparation/submission time; use that to decide which requirements are reasonable to insist on at submission versus after acceptance. Use time estimates to prioritize simplification efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools/templates
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal has many requirements for manuscript preparation, including unique styles, and it cannot limit them, can it provide the author a template that can save a significant amount of time/effort for both the author and the journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures: provide downloadable templates (Word, LaTeX), build or point to tools for metadata extraction and formatting, and consider automated conversions with manual checks to reduce author workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Have authors shared their feedback on any of the above aspects? Journals can administer short, occasional surveys to proactively seek feedback on the clarity/completeness of guidelines, the ease of following guidelines/using submission systems, and the time taken for manuscript preparation/submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periodic, short surveys or feedback channels to identify pain points and measure whether guideline/system changes reduce author burden. Incorporate diverse geographic and language perspectives, especially non–English-speaking authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global task force, audits, and accreditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute a global task force or committee on manuscript preparation/submission standards to define essential criteria for the quality of journal guidelines and submission systems; offer audits of journal systems/guidelines and provide a score or some form of accreditation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed composition: experienced journal editors, publishers, active researchers (including peer reviewers) across disciplines and geographies. Responsibilities: define minimum essential criteria (may vary by discipline), audit journals, accredit or score adherence, and encourage journals to avoid requiring more than the defined minimum at submission.
